newsitem.title: BOSNIA: World community leaders appeal to Bosnia's voters.
newsitem.headline: World community leaders appeal to Bosnia's voters.

text.p: Leaders of the international peace effort in Bosnia appealed to Bosnians on Friday to vote for peace and reconciliation in general elections on Saturday.

U.S. Admiral Joseph Lopez, commander of 53,000 NATO peace-keeping forces, international peace coordinator Carl Bildt, and Robert Frowick, who is overseeing the elections as regional director of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said in a joint message.
"We urge you all to approach election day with dignity, to consider your own choice carefully, and to know that your vote is a secret vote," they told Bosnia's Moslems, Serbs and Croats.
The statement said authorities in Bosnia's estranged Moslem, Serb and Croat-dominated ethnic entities had cooperated well to create conditions for voting in peace and security.
"We urge you to support their and our efforts. We will react with determination against any acts of manipulation or provocation," Lopez, Bildt and Frowick said.
"Tomorrow, the eyes of the world will be on Bosnia and on all of you. This is your day to show your national desire for peace, and your own personal and secret choice for a better future."
Voters will be choosing a multi-ethnic three-person presidency and united parliament, regional assemblies in the Moslem-Croat Federation and Serb Republic, and Federation cantonal councils.

Ethnic nationalist campaigning by the three main parties have raised fears that the elections will only seal Bosnia's division wrought by war as Moslems, Serbs and Croats argue over power-sharing arrangements.

A Gallup poll released this week showed that 44 percent of Serbs, 40 percent of Moslems and 36 percent of Croats expected the elections to solidify peace in Bosnia rather than exacerbate national tensions.
Twenty-two percent of Moslems, 20 percent of Serbs and 10 percent of Croats felt the vote would raise tensions.
Fifty-three percent of Croats and 28 percent each of Serbs and Moslems thought the elections would make no difference in their current relations, the survey found.

When Serbs and Croats, whose ultra-nationalist forces fought for sovereignty, were asked whether maintaining peace or gaining independence was more important, 74 percent of Serbs and 70 percent of Croats preferred peace.
